ui.footerTruth: One deterministic state. Every visual tells the same truth.

ui.nextStage: Next: stage the file, then commit the merge.

ui.timeEmpty: Ref and HEAD movements will appear here. Commits can remain recoverable even after a reset.
ui.tutorContext: The tutor can see branch tips, staged/working changes, conflicts and recent commands—never mutable state or file contents.
ui.grounded: Grounded in the current simulator snapshot
ui.rebaseIntro: Reword changes a message, squash combines a change with the previous commit, and drop removes it from replay. The engine applies every choice deterministically.
ui.hintIntro: Try the challenge first. Hints get progressively more specific.
ui.conceptQuestionA08: Which commit is the first bad commit in a bisect?
ui.conceptAnswerA08: The first commit whose test fails
ui.conceptDistractorA08: The newest commit on the branch
ui.conceptQuestionA09: What does a Git submodule store in its parent repository?
ui.conceptAnswerA09: A commit pointer to another repository
ui.conceptQuestionA10: Choose the correct Git object chain.

hero.title: Master Git by seeing what it actually does.
hero.subtitle: Learn branches, commits, merges and recovery through a real visual state machine — with an AI tutor that understands your current repo.

b01.title: Meet Git
b01.objective: Turn a normal folder into a Git repository.
b01.why: Git needs a repository before it can track history.
b01.mentalModel: A repository is the history system attached to your project folder.
hints: You need to initialize the folder.
Which command creates a Git repository?
Run `git init`.

b02.title: Your Three Git Zones
b02.objective: Stage `app.ts` and create your first commit.
b02.why: Most Git confusion disappears once these three zones are clear.
b02.mentalModel: You edit in the Working Tree, select versions in the Staging Area, and save those snapshots as commits.
hints: Your changed file is still only in the Working Tree.
Move the desired version into the Staging Area before committing.
Run `git add app.ts`, then `git commit -m "First snapshot"`.

b03.title: See Your History
b03.objective: Inspect history and identify the newest commit.
b03.why: Commits form a chain of saved project states.
b03.mentalModel: Each commit has an identity and parent relation, creating history.
hints: Use a command that shows commit history.
Try the compact one-line history.
Run `git log --oneline`.

b04.title: Branches Without Fear
b04.why: Branches let one line of work move without moving another.
b04.mentalModel: A branch is mainly a movable label pointing at a commit. HEAD says which branch you are working on.
hints: Create the branch label first.
Then move HEAD to that branch.
Run `git branch feature`, then `git switch feature`.

b05.title: Build on a Branch
b05.objective: Make two commits on `feature` while leaving `main` in place.
b05.why: This is the everyday reason branches exist.
b05.mentalModel: New commits move only the currently checked-out branch pointer.
hints: Check which branch HEAD is attached to.
Create and stage two separate changes.
Commit two separate changes while on `feature`.

b06.title: Bring Work Together
b06.why: A merge combines development lines. Sometimes Git only moves a pointer.
b06.mentalModel: If `main` has not diverged, a fast-forward simply moves `main` along existing commits.
hints: Switch to the branch that should receive the work.
Merge the source branch into the current branch.
Run `git switch main`, then `git merge feature`.

b07.title: Handle a Merge Conflict
b07.objective: Resolve the conflict in `app.ts` and finish the merge.
b07.why: Git asks for help only when it cannot safely choose the final content.
b07.mentalModel: Base is the shared past; ours and theirs changed the same place differently, so you choose the result.
hints: Inspect `git status` and the highlighted conflict file.
Choose final content, then stage the resolved file.
Resolve `app.ts`, run `git add app.ts`, then commit the merge.

b08.title: Undo Without Guessing
b08.objective: Use the appropriate undo strategy and see the difference.
b08.why: `reset` moves history refs; `revert` adds new correcting history.
b08.mentalModel: Ask whether history should move or whether a correcting commit should be added.
hints: Decide whether history may be rewritten.
Shared history is usually safer to correct with a new commit.
Use the requested reset mode or `git revert` and compare X-Ray before/after.

b09.title: Put Work Aside
b09.objective: Stash unfinished work, inspect it, then restore it.
b09.why: Stash gives you a clean worktree without committing unfinished work.
b09.mentalModel: Think of stash as a temporary shelf for local changes.
hints: Aim for a clean worktree without a new commit.
Put local changes on the stash stack.
Run `git stash`, inspect `git stash list`, then `git stash pop`.

b10.title: Understand Remotes
b10.objective: Synchronize the simulated local repository with `origin`.
b10.why: Local branches and remote-tracking branches are separate pointers.
b10.mentalModel: `fetch` updates your knowledge of the remote; `pull` integrates; `push` moves remote refs using local history.
hints: Fetch before deciding what the remote contains.
Watch `main` and `origin/main` as separate labels.
Run `git fetch origin`, then choose pull/push from ahead-behind state.

a01.title: Interactive Rebase
a01.objective: Turn noisy feature history into deliberate history.
a01.why: Interactive rebase lets you edit how local commits are replayed.
a01.mentalModel: Replaying changes creates new commit identities.
hints: Identify the local commits to rewrite.
Choose the correct rebase base.
Use pick/reword/squash/drop as the lesson requests.

a02.title: Cherry-Pick Surgery
a02.objective: Copy one specific change onto your current branch.
a02.why: Cherry-pick is useful when you want one change, not the whole source branch.
a02.mentalModel: Git replays the selected commit change on a new parent, creating a new identity.
hints: Find the source commit.
Replay that commit on the current branch.
Run `git cherry-pick <hash>`.

a03.title: Stash Like a Pro
a03.why: A stash stack is useful only when you know what each entry represents.
a03.mentalModel: Each stash is temporary local state associated with a base and stack order.
hints: Name the stash clearly.
Inspect the stack before applying.
Use `git stash -m "..."`, `git stash list`, then restore the intended entry.

a04.title: Reflog: Your Safety Net
a04.objective: Recover commits that vanished from normal branch history.
a04.why: Many scary Git mistakes only move references. Reflog remembers previous HEAD positions.
a04.mentalModel: A commit can be unreachable from a branch without immediately ceasing to exist.
hints: Inspect previous HEAD positions.
Find the lost tip in reflog.
Use `git reflog`, identify the old tip, then restore a branch/reference to it.

a05.title: Detached HEAD
a05.objective: Experiment from an old commit and save the work safely.
a05.why: Detached HEAD means HEAD points directly to a commit instead of a branch.
a05.mentalModel: Detached commits need a branch if you want an easy durable reference.
hints: Notice whether HEAD is attached to a branch.
Create a branch pointing at the experimental work.
Use `git switch -c rescue` before leaving the detached work.

a06.title: Advanced Merge Reasoning
a06.objective: Resolve a non-trivial merge using base, ours and theirs.
a06.why: Three-way merge becomes predictable when you inspect the shared base.
a06.mentalModel: Git compares both sides against the merge base and combines compatible changes.
hints: Identify the base and competing edits.
Resolve only the genuinely incompatible region.
Stage resolved files and complete the merge commit.

a07.title: Remote Divergence
a07.objective: Resolve a branch that is both ahead of and behind its remote.
a07.why: Fetch, pull and push make sense once local and remote-tracking refs are separate state.
a07.mentalModel: Divergence means each side has commits the other side lacks.
hints: Fetch before deciding remote state.
Inspect ahead/behind.
Integrate remote work before pushing when the remote cannot fast-forward.

a08.title: Git Bisect
a08.objective: Find a regression by repeatedly halving the suspect history.
a08.why: Binary search can dramatically reduce the number of commits you must test.
a08.mentalModel: Mark known-good and known-bad points, then test useful midpoints.
hints: Start with good/bad boundaries.
Classify the midpoint.
Repeat until the first bad commit remains.

a09.title: Submodules vs Subtrees
a09.objective: Understand two repository-composition approaches without pretending they are the same.
a09.why: Both connect projects, but ownership/update mechanics differ.
a09.mentalModel: A submodule records a pointer to another repo state; a subtree brings another project content into your history.
hints: Focus on where nested history lives.
Compare pointer-based composition with integrated content.
Classify each visual scenario as submodule or subtree.

a10.title: Git Internals
a10.objective: Trace a file from blob to tree to commit to branch ref.
a10.why: Git becomes less magical once you see that commits point to trees and refs point to commits.
a10.mentalModel: Content objects are immutable; movable refs name points in that object graph.
hints: Start from file content.
Follow blob → tree → commit.
Then identify the ref that gives the commit a human-friendly name.
